title: How Coding Agents change Software Development Forever - Hailong Zhang

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is coding agents—Guru generates unit test PRs, and the discussion covers Copilot, Cursor, and an Agent OS for software-engineering tasks. Guru is a coding assistant embedded in PR workflows, and the Agent OS serves as a developer platform for building new SE agents. Guru is deployed in production with reported PR acceptance rates and commit statistics. The talk assumes familiarity with GitHub workflows and unit testing but does not require deep ML expertise. summary: Hailong Zhang explores how coding agents reshape software development across three themes: the future workflow, a practical unit test agent example, and the engineering of agents. He argues generative AI will handle routine work—entry-level coding, debugging, testing, and operations—while humans retain creative responsibilities like product and architecture design. The future workflow envisions multiple small agents embedded across repositories and pipeline stages, handling unit tests, bug fixes, documentation, code reviews, and releases. Zhang distinguishes two collaboration modes. Synchronous agents like GitHub Copilot and Cursor live inside the IDE, working alongside developers in real time; these have been available since 2020, matured since 2023, and are widely adopted by 2024. Asynchronous agents, emerging in 2024, operate as autonomous bots triggered manually or automatically, completing tasks without human attention and submitting deliverables. The core example is Guru (Test Gru), an agent that generates and manages unit tests. Triggered by pull requests, Guru detects code changes, determines whether new or modified tests are needed, writes and runs tests, and submits a PR with coverage summaries. Zhang notes unit tests are increasingly important because AI-assisted coding tools generate code rapidly, making bugs easy to overlook. In production, over 50% of Guru's PRs are accepted by humans, and it handles approximately 80% of unit tests in its own repo, making it the top contributor by commit count. On building agents, Zhang emphasizes defining clear, concrete, doable problems first, then constructing evaluation datasets and harnesses. Guru runs on multiple frontier LLMs—OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google—selecting different models for different stages and fine-tuning GPT-4 with human-labeled unit test code. Context building is critical: per-language and per-framework contexts are assembled from GitHub issues, code reviews, commits, PRs, READMEs, and code. To scale beyond unit tests to refactoring and E2E testing, the team built an agent operating system that abstracts shared runtime, tools, and context, enabling rapid agent creation across software engineering tasks.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Future Software Development Workflow
sections.summary: Zhang introduces the talk and discusses how generative AI will handle routine coding, debugging, testing, and operating tasks while humans retain creative work. He distinguishes synchronous agents (Copilot, Cursor, IDE-integrated, available since 2020) from asynchronous agents (autonomous bots, emerging 2024) and envisions a future workflow with many small agents across repos handling unit tests, bug fixes, documentation, code reviews, and releases.

sections.title: Unit Test Agent Example: Guru
sections.summary: Zhang presents Guru (Test Gru), an AI agent that generates and manages unit tests. Triggered manually or by pull requests, Guru detects code changes, determines if tests are needed, writes and runs tests, and submits a PR with test summaries and coverage information. Human review is required before merging. Zhang argues unit tests are more important in the AI era because fast AI-generated code can introduce overlooked bugs, yet developers dislike writing tests.

sections.title: Performance, Building Agents, and Agent OS
sections.summary: Zhang shares Guru's production performance: over 50% PR acceptance rate, ~80% of unit tests handled in its own repo, and top contributor by commit count. He details the agent-building process: defining clear problems, building evaluation datasets and harnesses, working with multiple frontier LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google) for different stages, fine-tuning GPT-4 with human-labeled test code, and engineering per-language/framework contexts from repos and GitHub artifacts. He introduces an agent OS that abstracts shared infrastructure to enable rapid agent creation for refactoring, E2E testing, and other SE tasks.
